title: Augustine and the Puzzle of Time
objective: After this level you can explain Augustine's puzzle that the past is gone, the future not yet here and the present has no length, and his answer in the mind.
summary: Augustine found that past, future and a lengthless present all seem not to exist, and placed time in the mind as memory, attention and expectation; Aristotle had tied time to change instead.

cards.headline: You know exactly what time is. Until someone asks you.
cards.body: Augustine of Hippo admitted exactly that, then turned the embarrassment into one of philosophy’s great puzzles.

cards.headline: If no one asks me
cards.body: In Book 11 of his Confessions, Augustine writes: “What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.” We talk about time all day and understand each other perfectly. The trouble starts only when you try to say what it actually is.

cards.headline: Time keeps vanishing
cards.body: Look for time and it slips away. The past is no longer. The future is not yet. That leaves the present, but any stretch of it, a year, a day, an hour, splits into parts already past and parts still to come. Keep slicing and what’s left has no length at all: “The present hath no space.” And a present that never passed into the past wouldn’t be time. It would be eternity.

cards.headline: Time lives in the mind
cards.body: Augustine’s answer: past, present and future exist as three presents in the soul. Memory is the present of things past, attention (“sight”) of things present, expectation of things future. Recite a psalm you know by heart: at first expectation covers the whole, then it shrinks as memory grows, until it has all passed into memory. Time, he concludes, is a distention, a stretching, of the soul itself.

cards.headline: A rival clock
cards.body: Aristotle had tied time to the world instead. There is no time without change, he held, and time is the measure of change: a falling leaf can go faster or slower, but time itself can’t. Aristotle also asked whether time would exist without a mind to count it; if only a mind can count, he answered, there could be change but no time. Augustine’s account is often called subjectivist: he locates time in the mind’s memory, attention and expectation.

cards.headline: Augustine and the Puzzle of Time: the big picture
learned: What is time? Easy until someone asks
Past gone, future not yet, present lengthless
Aristotle: time is the measure of change

questions.prompt: According to Augustine, what is the present of things past?

options.label: Expectation
options.rationale: That’s the present of things future.

options.label: Attention
options.rationale: That’s the present of things present.

options.label: Eternity
options.rationale: Eternity is a present that never passes.

questions.explanation: Augustine’s three presents: memory for things past, attention for things present, expectation for things future.

questions.prompt: How does reciting a psalm show Augustine’s view of time at work?

options.label: The words are timed by the movement of the sun
options.rationale: He finds time in the soul, not the sky.

options.label: As the words pass, expectation shrinks and memory grows
The psalm has no length until it is written down
Every word lasts exactly as long as the one before
options.rationale: He is not measuring equal words.

questions.explanation: Expectation first covers the whole psalm; as each word passes through attention, expectation shrinks and memory grows. Time is that stretching of the soul.

questions.prompt: Augustine says a present that never passed would be eternity, not time. What did Plato, in Level 4, call eternal and changeless?

options.label: The things we see and touch
The five aggregates of a person
The Forms, such as Beauty and Justice
The shadows on the cave wall
options.rationale: Shadows are the least real of all.

questions.explanation: Plato ranked the eternal, changeless Forms, such as Beauty, Justice and Equality, above the changing world.
